questions.stem: Which of these is an example of continuous data?

options.text: Number of students in a class
Number of cars in a car park

questions.explanation: Height is continuous because it can take any value within a range and is measured rather than counted. Number of students and cars are discrete; shoe size is also discrete.

options.text: Can take any value within a range
Can only take specific, separate values

questions.explanation: Discrete data can only take specific, separate values (usually whole numbers obtained by counting), such as the number of siblings.

questions.stem: Which of these is qualitative (categorical) data?
questions.explanation: Favourite colour is qualitative because it describes a quality or category, not a numerical measurement.

questions.stem: Time taken to run 100 metres is an example of:
questions.explanation: Time is continuous because it can take any value within a range (e.g. 11.32 seconds, 11.327 seconds) and is measured, not counted.

questions.stem: Which type of data is 'number of pets owned by each student'?
questions.explanation: Number of pets is counted in whole numbers (0, 1, 2, 3, ...), making it discrete quantitative data.

questions.stem: The key difference between quantitative and qualitative data is:

options.text: Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is descriptive
Qualitative data can be measured numerically

questions.explanation: Quantitative data is numerical (it can be measured or counted), while qualitative data describes qualities or categories (such as colour or type).

questions.stem: Why is it important to know whether data is discrete or continuous?

options.text: It does not matter -- all data is treated the same
It affects the choice of chart and how class intervals are written
Continuous data cannot be displayed on charts
Discrete data cannot have averages calculated

questions.explanation: The type of data determines which charts to use (e.g. bar charts for discrete, histograms for continuous) and how class intervals are written (e.g. using inequality notation for continuous data).
